sources.title: Su Song (Q1265657), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-01): label 'Su Song', description 'Chinese polymath and statesman (1020-1101)', birth 1020, death 1101, Korean label 소송, image 'Su Song full-length' album picture. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Su Song' (public introduction paragraph opened; the rest of the entry is subscriber-only). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Su Song (born 1020 Fujian, died 1101 Kaifeng) was a Chinese scholar and administrative and financial expert in the imperial bureaucracy; his Illustrated Pharmacopoeia (1070) revealed his knowledge of drugs, zoology, metallurgy and related technology; an armillary clock he built to serve as the basis of calendrical reform was housed in a 35-foot (11 m) tower and powered by a waterwheel and chain drive, with a mechanism that anticipated techniques not used in Europe for hundreds of years. Encyclopaedic reference; the 'anticipated Europe' wording is retrospective praise and is not carded.

Song Shi (History of Song), chapter 340, biography of Su Song (compiled in the Yuan dynasty, about 1345; Chinese Wikisource transcription), read in full for the Su Song section: official career in provincial and court posts; commissioned to make a new armillary sphere and put in charge; used the Ministry of Personnel clerk Han Gonglian, who understood calculation and had ingenuity; a three-tier tower with an armillary sphere above, a celestial globe in the middle and a time-announcing section below, linked by one mechanism that turned wheels with flowing water without human power; and a closing assessment that he was broad-minded, self-restrained by ritual and law, lived plainly despite high rank, and was versed in classics, histories, harmonics, star officials, mathematics, mountain-and-river texts and materia medica. Written about 250 years after his death in the genre of official eulogy; administrative and political episodes in it are NOT scored.

Xinhua Daily Telegraph (Yi Yangang and Yan Zhihong), 'Some say Leonardo da Vinci was the Western Su Song; so who was Su Song?' (news.cn, 20 June 2025), read through a fetched summary of the article: a Northern Song statesman, astronomer, pharmacologist, mechanical engineer and poet; he led the water-powered armillary-sphere and clock tower with a team of skilled craftsmen including Han Gonglian and Wang Yizhi, over more than three years; a three-tier tower with armillary sphere, rotating celestial globe and time-keeping gear train; his Xin Yixiang Fayao is described as a very early illustrated machine manual; the 21-volume Bencao Tujing took about four years, covers 780 medicines with 933 illustrations and is called the earliest printed herbal with specimen illustrations; he had local officials identify and draw medicinal materials; Needham is quoted on the combination of clockwork and observing armillary sphere; the article also remarks that astronomy served imperial legitimacy and limited public access. A celebratory modern popular article; its 'world first' wording is not carded.

Sarina (Shanghai Jiao Tong University), 'How Ancient China Encouraged Technological Innovation: The Song Dynasty's Science Rewards', People's Forum, 1 August 2022 (paper.people.com.cn), read through a fetched summary: Su Song initiated and organised the 1088 water-powered armillary sphere and clock tower, selected talent without regard to rank and put the low-ranking Han Gonglian, strong in astronomy and calculation, directly on the team; the tower's opening roof, daily-rotating globe and anchor-shaped escapement are noted; Needham is quoted that it may be the direct ancestor of medieval European astronomical clocks. Celebratory, no criticism offered; used only to corroborate the Han Gonglian recruitment.

Wikipedia, 'Su Song' (raw wikitext read for orientation and for the citations it points to: Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 4 part 2; the observation that the tower was a government project that did not lead to mass-produced clocks (Derk Bodde, as cited there); and the dates 1088 model, 1090 bronze casting, 1094 completion). Orientation only; never counted as a substantive source or used as support for a row.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_susong_songshi, src_susong_britannica, src_susong_xinhua | c.1050-1100 | Yuan-era official history, encyclopedia, modern press] The Song Shi closes his biography by saying he was versed in classics, histories, harmonics, star officials, mathematics, mountain-and-river texts and materia medica; Britannica credits him with the 1070 Illustrated Pharmacopoeia (drugs, zoology, metallurgy) and an armillary clock built as the basis of calendrical reform; Xinhua lists pharmacology, astronomy and mechanical engineering. The breadth of output (a pharmacopoeia and a clock-tower project) is documented, but the Song Shi sentence is a conventional eulogy, the press pieces are celebratory, and nothing shows how he moved between fields. Political and administrative offices are NOT scored. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as the top-risk row; lowered from 68 / 0.48 to 64 / 0.44 because the breadth claim rests on a formulaic eulogy plus celebratory press and only Britannica independently confirms two fields.

collaboration.rationale: [src_susong_songshi, src_susong_xinhua, src_susong_peoplesforum | 1080s | official history, modern press] The Song Shi says that, put in charge of the new armillary sphere, he took the Ministry of Personnel clerk Han Gonglian, who understood calculation and had ingenuity, and had him build the tower; Xinhua says he led a team of craftsmen including Han Gonglian and Wang Yizhi for more than three years; the People's Forum article says he picked Han Gonglian regardless of his low rank. The Han Gonglian recruitment is repeated across all three, but the two press articles may simply retell the official history, so the evidence is one documented pattern, not three independent episodes; how the team actually worked is not described.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_susong_songshi, src_susong_xinhua, src_susong_britannica | 1080s-1090s | official history, press, encyclopedia] The Song Shi describes a tower planned as three tiers (armillary sphere, globe, time-announcing section) coupled to one water-driven mechanism; Xinhua says construction took more than three years and that he wrote a treatise with drawings of the whole instrument and its parts, and that he had local officials identify and illustrate medicinal materials for the herbal; Britannica says the clock was built to serve a calendrical-reform purpose. These are consistent with deliberate, staged planning of a large instrument and a large compilation, but the plans themselves and the working schedule are not documented in the sources read, so confidence is low.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_susong_songshi, src_susong_britannica | 1050s-1090s | official history, encyclopedia] The Song Shi says he was deeply versed in calendrical science and harmonics and was consulted by the court on institutional matters, and Britannica describes an armillary clock built to serve calendrical reform and a pharmacopoeia that showed deep knowledge of drugs and metallurgy. This is consistent with sustained deepening of technical expertise across his career, but the evidence is retrospective, the court-consultation part is administrative and is not scored, and no source describes his own study habits first-hand.

PERSPECTIVES: imperial-era official history (Song Shi, a Yuan compilation about 250 years later), encyclopaedic reference (Britannica), two modern state-media popular articles (Xinhua, People's Forum). There is no first-hand source on his working behaviour beyond the Song Shi.
